Theodore Roosevelt at 21, in his own words.

In the fall of 1879 he was a senior at Harvard. His diary for Wednesday 12 November records a drive out to the Saltonstalls, the family whose home in Chestnut Hill was where he had met Alice Hathaway Lee the year before. Then he took stock of college life.

He spent most of his spare time "in the club," he wrote, and went "a good deal" to the Alpha Delta Phi, where the members were "very pleasant and intellectual," which he called "a rare thing with college boys."

Then this:

"I have been off on a great many sprees this year, and have been studying well and keeping late hours; thanks to the magnificent condition I am in after the summer I seem to stand it pretty well."

That summer he had gone back to the Maine woods and climbed Mount Katahdin with the guides Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow. Five years later, Sewall and Dow came west to help run Roosevelt's Elkhorn Ranch in the Dakota Badlands.

He was also courting Alice. She said yes in January.

The diary page survives in the Theodore Roosevelt Papers at the Library of Congress and is shown here, along with his room in Cambridge and a photograph taken that May of Alice, her cousin Rose Saltonstall, and Theodore.

#OTD 13 Nov 1905. British hunter F. C. Selous stays at the White House. Before dinner, Theodore Roosevelt gets him to tell "delightfully exciting lion and hyena stories to Ethel, Archie and Quentin."

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/post-presidency/african-safari

Lion stories at the White House.

On Monday 13 November 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt had a houseguest he admired: Frederick Courteney Selous, the British hunter and explorer. Selous had spent decades in southern Africa, a career that included guiding Cecil Rhodes's 1890 expedition into what became Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe.

"He is a perfect old dear; just as simple and natural as can be and very interesting," Roosevelt wrote to his son Kermit a few days later.

In the afternoon Roosevelt took him "for a good scramble and climb" with a party that included Gifford Pinchot. Before dinner, he wrote, he got Selous "to spend three-quarters of an hour in telling delightfully exciting lion and hyena stories to Ethel, Archie and Quentin."

"He told them most vividly and so enthralled the little boys that the next evening I had to tell them a large number myself."

Some of those stories the children already knew from their father reading them aloud, as he recalled years later in his Autobiography. Once Selous told them, he admitted, "my own rendering of the incidents was cast entirely into the shade."

In 1909 Roosevelt went to Africa himself, and Selous was there too. The two of them rode the front of a train together in British East Africa that year, shown here.

#OTD 14 November 1902. On a Mississippi bear hunt, guide Holt Collier stuns a bear, sends for Theodore Roosevelt, and ropes it to a tree for him to shoot. He refuses, and has it put out of its misery.

A newspaper cartoon followed, then a toy: the teddy bear.

#OTD 14 Nov 1902. In Mississippi, guide Holt Collier ropes a stunned bear to a tree for Theodore Roosevelt to shoot. He refuses. A newspaper cartoon follows, then a toy: the teddy bear.

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/legacy/teddy-bear

The real story behind the teddy bear is rougher than the toy.

On 14 November 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt was on a bear hunt in the Mississippi Delta, near Smedes. His guide was Holt Collier, born enslaved and by then a renowned bear hunter in the Delta. Roosevelt later wrote that Collier had spent half a century hunting bears, "having killed or assisted in killing over three thousand bears."

The president had no luck that day. While he was back at camp for lunch, Collier's hounds ran a bear into a water hole. The exhausted animal killed one of the dogs. Collier struck it with his rifle and sent word for Roosevelt. Meanwhile he roped the bear and tied it to a tree.

Roosevelt arrived to find a stunned, bloodied bear tied up and waiting for him. He refused to shoot it. He had it put out of its misery instead, and it was killed with a knife.

He was not pleased. Writing to a friend later that month, he called it "a most unsatisfactory experience in a bear hunt in Mississippi," and said his hosts had turned the outing into "a cross between a hunt and a picnic."

The newspapers saw it differently. Clifford Berryman drew the scene for the front page of The Washington Post, captioned "Drawing the Line in Mississippi." In the cartoon the bear looks like a cub. The real one, newspapers reported, was a grown bear of more than 200 pounds.

In Brooklyn, shopkeepers Morris and Rose Michtom made a stuffed bear; family accounts say they called it "Teddy's bear." Within a few years, toy bears were a national craze.

Holt Collier has his own legacy. The Holt Collier National Wildlife Refuge in the Mississippi Delta bears his name; the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service calls it the only national wildlife refuge named for an African American.

#OTD 15 Nov 1906. 120 years ago, Theodore Roosevelt comes ashore in Panama to inspect the canal, in the rain. The State Department records it as the first visit abroad by a sitting president.

#OTD 15 November 1906. 120 years ago, Theodore Roosevelt comes ashore in Panama to inspect the canal: the first visit abroad by a sitting president.

He chose November "partly because it is the rainiest month of the year," and it rained for three days.

120 years ago today, a president of the United States stepped ashore in a foreign country to see a job for himself.

The battleship Louisiana reached Colón, Panama, a day early, on the afternoon of Wednesday 14 November 1906. On Thursday morning, 15 November, Theodore Roosevelt came ashore to inspect the Panama Canal. The State Department records the trip as the first visit abroad by a sitting president. The Canal Zone had come under American control after Panama broke away from Colombia in 1903, with American support.

He picked the season on purpose. "I chose the month of November for my visit partly because it is the rainiest month of the year, the month in which the work goes forward at the greatest disadvantage, and one of the two months which the medical department of the French Canal Company found most unhealthy," he told Congress afterward.

It was raining when he came ashore, and the rain hardly let up for three days.

That first day, by his own report, he toured the bay by tug, inspected Ancon Hospital, and dropped in for a meal without notice. "I myself took dinner at the La Boca government hotel, no warning whatever having been given of my coming," he wrote. His meal, he said, was "excellent." The 30-cent meal at those hotels ran to soup, beef, mashed potatoes, peas, beets, chili con carne and plum pudding.

Those hotels served the canal's white American employees. Most of the canal's labor force, tens of thousands of workers, came from the West Indies, and they were paid and housed separately.

The next morning he climbed into the cab of one of the 95-ton steam shovels as the rain came on, and that photograph is shown here too.

#OTD 125 years ago, 18 November 1901: Secretary of State John Hay and Lord Pauncefote sign the treaty that lets the United States build a canal on its own, with no ban on fortifying it.

As governor of New York, Theodore Roosevelt had opposed the first version. "I do not see why we should dig the canal if we are not to fortify it so as to insure its being used for ourselves and against our foes in time of war," he wrote.

125 years ago today, two diplomats signed a treaty in Washington that cleared the way for the United States to build a canal between the oceans.

On 18 November 1901, Secretary of State John Hay and the British ambassador, Lord Pauncefote, signed the second Hay–Pauncefote Treaty. It replaced the Clayton–Bulwer Treaty of 1850, under which Britain and the United States had each promised never to take exclusive control of a Central American canal, or to fortify one.

Theodore Roosevelt had been president for two months. He had also publicly opposed the first version.

Hay and Pauncefote had signed an earlier treaty in February 1900. It let the United States build and run a canal, but kept it open to the warships of every nation in war as in peace, and it barred fortifications. Roosevelt, then governor of New York, objected in public, and drew a private letter of protest from Hay. Privately he wrote to the naval strategist Alfred Thayer Mahan: "I do not see why we should dig the canal if we are not to fortify it so as to insure its being used for ourselves and against our foes in time of war."

The Senate amended that treaty. Britain refused the amendments, and Hay went back to the table.

The new treaty expressly set aside the 1850 agreement and left out the ban on fortifications. It still opened the canal to the ships of all nations "on terms of entire equality." The Senate approved it on 16 December 1901.

It left the route open. Most of Washington still expected Nicaragua. Within two years the choice was Panama, and that is a story for another day.

Shown here: John Hay, about 1901–02, and Roosevelt at his desk as governor of New York.

The Senate amended that treaty. Britain refused the amendments, and Hay went back to the table.

Two weeks after losing the 1912 presidential election, Theodore Roosevelt wrote to London.

His letter of 19 November 1912 went to Millicent Garrett Fawcett, president of Britain's National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies. That August she had cabled him her "cordial congratulations" after the new Progressive Party came out for votes for women. Its platform pledged "equal suffrage to men and women alike" at a time when most American women could not vote for president.

Roosevelt had finished second, behind Woodrow Wilson and ahead of President Taft.

"Indeed, I feel that although we were beaten at the polls, we Progressives did help forward the movement for social and industrial justice in this country," he told her. "We particularly helped the woman suffrage cause by actually using the best women in the country on an exact equality with the men in doing the work."

Then he told her what he had planned: "If I had come into power I intended to put women in two or three places in my administration, with the ultimate hope of getting one of them, probably Miss Jane Addams, into the Cabinet…" Not right away, he added.

Jane Addams, co-founder of Hull House in Chicago, had seconded his nomination at the Progressive convention that August. In 1931 she became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, the prize Roosevelt had won in 1906.

No woman sat in a president's Cabinet until Frances Perkins became Secretary of Labor in 1933. The Nineteenth Amendment, guaranteeing women the vote nationwide, was ratified in 1920.

A copy of the letter survives in the Theodore Roosevelt Papers at the Library of Congress.

On the afternoon of 20 November 1908, President Theodore Roosevelt skipped his ride to talk about Africa.

His visitor was Carl Akeley, the Field Museum's chief taxidermist, who had first gone collecting in Africa in 1896. Roosevelt, about three and a half months from leaving office, was planning a year-long safari for the Smithsonian. The next day's Washington Evening Star reported that instead of taking a ride, the president "indulged in a long talk about his African trip," with Akeley holding his attention for half an hour.

Akeley was getting ready for an expedition of his own, to collect a group of elephants for the American Museum of Natural History in New York. He asked Roosevelt to shoot one or two for the museum if he got the chance, and Roosevelt said he would if it were possible.

A year later, almost to the week, Roosevelt's party was camped near the 'Nzoi River on the Uasin Gishu plateau in British East Africa when, as Roosevelt told it, a familiar figure turned up on the trail. It was Akeley.

"A year previously Mr. and Mrs. Akeley had lunched with me at the White House, and we had talked over our proposed African trips," Roosevelt wrote in African Game Trails. The next morning the two men went after a herd of elephants together. Roosevelt shot a cow for the museum group, and his son Kermit shot a calf.

The museum's hall of African mammals now bears Akeley's name. A cow from that hunt is reported to stand among the eight elephants at its center.

Shown here: Roosevelt and Akeley after that hunt, 1909, photographed by Leslie Tarlton and by Kermit Roosevelt.

Around this date in 1908, a cleaning at the White House turned up trouble with a painting the White House Historical Association calls "the most famous and important painting in the White House."

Archie Butt, the president's military aide, described it in a letter dated 24 November. Two or three days earlier, he wrote, the shades had been raised high to clean the rooms, and "for the first time in several months everything in the Red Room was visible."

Over the Red Room fireplace hung Gilbert Stuart's full-length portrait of George Washington, the picture Dolley Madison, by her own account, refused to leave behind as the British closed in on Washington in 1814. She ordered the frame broken and the canvas taken out.

"Much to the consternation of everyone, it was discovered that the portrait of Washington by Stuart was in such wretched condition that the canvas was separating," Butt wrote.

Edith Roosevelt, he reported, ordered it sent out to be restored. She "regards it as the most valuable possession of the White House and is greatly distressed over its condition."

Bought for the President's House in 1800, the portrait is the only object remaining in the White House from the John Adams years, according to the White House Historical Association. It hangs today in the East Room.

Twenty degrees below zero.

That is what Theodore Roosevelt's thermometer read on 22 November 1884, the day he rode from the Maltese Cross ranch into town and back with Bill Sewall. His diary entry is short: six sharptail grouse shot, a cold ride, "thermometer 20° below zero."

He was 26, back in the Badlands for a few early-winter weeks, nine months after his wife and his mother died on the same day in New York. He was not just passing time. The next day he told his sister Anna he was trying to start a stockmen's association.

The cattlemen of the Little Missouri shared open range. Their herds mixed, roundups needed planning, brands needed recording, and there were thieves to worry about. There was no one to set rules but the ranchers themselves. Others, Howard Eaton among them, had tried to organize earlier that year.

In the days that followed, as biographer Hermann Hagedorn tells it, Roosevelt and Sewall rode from ranch to ranch along the valley, making the case. On 19 December 1884, representatives of eleven cattle outfits met in Medora and organized the Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association. They elected Roosevelt chairman.

A little over a year earlier he had come west as a New York hunter after buffalo. Now the stockmen of the Little Missouri had chosen him to run their meetings.

#OTD 24 Nov 1908: Theodore Roosevelt creates the Dakota National Forest, about 14,000 acres of pine country in what is now Slope County, ND. Same day: Ocala NF, Florida. Wilson abolished it in 1917.

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/presidency/conservation/national-forests

North Dakota once had a national forest.

In the badlands of what is now Slope County, up the Little Missouri from Medora, there are scattered stands of ponderosa pine. On 24 November 1908, Theodore Roosevelt signed a proclamation setting aside about 14,000 acres of that country, some 22 sections, as the Dakota National Forest.

The proclamation is a few sentences long. It says the public lands there were "in part covered with timber," and that "the public good would be promoted by utilizing said lands as a National Forest." The same day, Roosevelt signed a second proclamation creating the Ocala National Forest in Florida.

According to the State Historical Society of North Dakota, Governor John Burke had brought the pines to the Forest Service's attention, and a forester came out to look them over that summer. A quarter century after Roosevelt first came to the Little Missouri, the pines upriver from his old range were under federal protection.

The forest did not last. A tree nursery was started there in 1912, but on 30 July 1917 President Woodrow Wilson abolished the Dakota National Forest by proclamation. Some of that country lies within today's Little Missouri National Grassland.

Shown here: the Forest Service diagram of the Dakota National Forest and the text of Roosevelt's proclamation, both from Volume 35 of the U.S. Statutes at Large.

Tomorrow is Thanksgiving. On Thanksgiving Day 1880, four weeks after his wedding, Theodore Roosevelt hosted dinner for New York's newsboys.

"Emlen and I gave the newsboys a big dinner; about a hundred came," he wrote in his diary on 25 November 1880. Emlen was his first cousin, William Emlen Roosevelt.

The dinner was his father's tradition. Theodore Roosevelt Sr. was a close friend of Charles Loring Brace, whose Children's Aid Society ran the Newsboys' Lodging House, where boys who sold papers on the street could get a cheap bed, a wash and a meal. In his Autobiography, Roosevelt recalled that on Thanksgiving or Christmas his father "was always back in time to go to the dinner at the Newsboys' Lodging-House." "At a very early age we children were taken with him and were required to help."

His father had died in February 1878. Now 22, a Columbia law student and newly married to Alice Hathaway Lee, Roosevelt kept the custom going. That evening the family sat down to its own Thanksgiving. "We had a great family dinner in the evening," he wrote; "Alice looked like a little Queen."

Years later, Roosevelt noted that when he was president, the governor of Alaska, John Green Brady, was one of those former newsboys, sent west as a boy by Brace and by Roosevelt's father.

#OTD Thanksgiving, 26 November 1908: the Roosevelts' last Thanksgiving in the White House.

Quentin, 11, was just out of a leg cast. "He roller-skated; he practised football," his father wrote, and "he went to the slaughter-house and got a pig for Thanksgiving dinner."

The menu: a turkey of more than 25 pounds, the roast pig, and ice cream shaped like quail.

Thanksgiving fell on 26 November in 1908, too. It was the Roosevelts' last one in the White House.

Quentin, who had turned 11 the week before, had just had his leg taken out of a plaster cast, and he made up for lost time. His father wrote to Archie, away at school, the next day:

"His leg was out of plaster and there was nothing he did not do. He roller-skated; he practised football; he had engineering work and electrical work; he went all around the city; he romped all over the White House; he went to the slaughter-house and got a pig for Thanksgiving dinner."

That evening was a family dinner: the President and Edith, Ethel, Quentin, Alice and Nick Longworth, and a few others. One was Captain Archie Butt, the President's military aide, who wrote a long letter to his sister-in-law Clara about it.

Butt's menu: creamed pea soup, then the biggest turkey he had ever seen, a little over 25 pounds dressed. Behind it came a roast pig with an apple in its mouth. When Quentin asked whether there would be vegetables, out came spinach, sugared sweet potatoes and rice. Then a salad of lettuce and avocado ("alligator pears"), apple and mince pies, and ice cream molded in the shape of quail, with melted brown sugar poured over for gravy.

When the waiter began to serve the sherry, Edith told him that since it was Thanksgiving he could serve champagne. Butt said he had never seen anything stronger than sherry or Rhine wine on that table except at formal dinners. The President, he wrote, told one story after another all through dinner.

In March the family left the White House for good.

Shown here: the President with Archie and Quentin, about 1904; Archie and Quentin at play, about 1904 (Library of Congress); and "A Thanksgiving Truce," a 1905 Puck cartoon of Roosevelt at a holiday table with the animals.

#OTD 27 November 1905: Mark Twain comes to lunch at the White House, three days before his 70th birthday.

The New York Times called it "purely social." It wasn't. He came to press Theodore Roosevelt about atrocities in King Leopold's Congo. Afterward he wrote Edith Roosevelt that the matter "was on my citizen-conscience & must be unloaded."

Mark Twain came to lunch at the White House on 27 November 1905, three days before his 70th birthday.

The New York Times put it on the front page the next morning and called the visit "purely social." It was not.

Twain had come about the Congo. Under King Leopold II of Belgium, the Congo Free State was run as his personal possession, worked for rubber, and reports of forced labor, mutilation and killing had been reaching Europe and America for years. Twain was an honorary vice president of the American Congo Reform Association, and that September it had published his King Leopold's Soliloquy, a furious satire in the king's own voice.

So Twain sat down to lunch with the President, the First Lady and a few guests, and found a private word with Roosevelt about the Congo. According to Twain scholar Hunt Hawkins, Roosevelt showed interest and said he would ask Assistant Secretary of State Robert Bacon for a report. Bacon wrote to Twain a week later, asking what England had already done.

The next day Twain wrote to Edith Roosevelt to explain himself. "I am a citizen," he wrote, "& the matter was on my citizen-conscience & must be unloaded."

The two did not always get along. Twain said sharp things about Roosevelt over the years, much of it in private. On this day they shared a table, and Twain got his hearing.

In 1899 Theodore Roosevelt published The Rough Riders, his own account of the regiment he led in Cuba. It was told very, very much in the first person.

Thanksgiving fell on 30 November in 1905, and the Roosevelts spent it in the Virginia woods.

#OTD 1 December 1898: Governor-elect Theodore Roosevelt asks Senator Henry Cabot Lodge to chase down his Medal of Honor recommendation: "Now, one of my usual worrying requests!"

Five days later he wrote: "I am entitled to the Medal of Honor, and I want it."

It was awarded in 2001, posthumously.

Theodore Roosevelt had been elected governor of New York three weeks earlier. On 1 December 1898, from Sagamore Hill, he wrote his closest friend, Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, about state business, including whether to put a machine politician in charge of the state's canals.

Then he turned to what was really on his mind:

"Now, one of my usual worrying requests! On Sept. 17th Meiklejohn wrote me that there was in the War Department the recommendation for me for the medal of honor, by Wood, Wheeler and Shafter. Can you get me a copy of it? Can you get any idea as to when they are likely to take action?"

George Meiklejohn was the Assistant Secretary of War. Leonard Wood, Joseph Wheeler and William Shafter were his commanders in Cuba, and they had put him in for the medal for 1 July 1898, when he led the charge up Kettle Hill and on across the San Juan Heights.

Lodge's reply brought word of a discouraging remark about the medals from Secretary of War Russell Alger, with whom Roosevelt was already on bad terms. On 6 December Roosevelt fired back with a long account of his own conduct under fire:

"I don't ask this as a favor—I ask it as a right."

And near the end: "I am entitled to the Medal of Honor, and I want it."

Lodge, meanwhile, had gone to the War Department in person, and on 5 December he reported that officials there expected the medal to come "as a matter of course."

The medal never came in his lifetime. On 16 January 2001, more than a century after the charge, President Bill Clinton awarded Theodore Roosevelt the Medal of Honor posthumously. It is on view at the Library in Medora.

Letters quoted from Selections from the Correspondence of Theodore Roosevelt and Henry Cabot Lodge (1925).

Shown here: Colonel Roosevelt after his return from Cuba, 1898; Roosevelt and the Rough Riders on the heights they took, July 1898 (William Dinwiddie); and Henry Cabot Lodge, about 1912 (all Library of Congress).

A hundred and forty years ago today, on 2 December 1886, Theodore Roosevelt married Edith Kermit Carow at St. George's, Hanover Square, in London. The fog was so thick that day that, by biographers' accounts, it filled the church.

They had known each other almost all their lives. Edith grew up near the Roosevelts in New York and was a close friend of his sister Corinne. Then Theodore married Alice Hathaway Lee, and in February 1884 Alice died, two days after giving birth to their daughter, on the same day as his mother.

He went west to his ranches on the Little Missouri. In the fall of 1885, back in New York, he and Edith met again, and that November they became secretly engaged. When the newspapers got wind of it the next September, he wrote to his sister Bamie to confirm it:

"I am engaged to Edith and before Christmas I shall cross the ocean and marry her."

In the same letter he was hard on himself: "I utterly disbelieve in and disapprove of second marriages; I have always considered that they argued weakness in a man's character."

He married her anyway. A few days after losing the race for mayor of New York, he sailed for England with Bamie. On the crossing he met a young British diplomat, Cecil Spring Rice, who agreed to be his best man. Spring Rice also talked the groom into wearing bright orange gloves.

The wedding was small, followed by a long wedding trip through England, France and Italy. They were married for 32 years and raised six children: Alice, and their own five, Ted, Kermit, Ethel, Archie and Quentin. Spring Rice stayed a lifelong friend, and later served as British ambassador in Washington.

Shown here: Roosevelt in 1885, in a studio portrait in the buckskins of his Dakota years; Edith Roosevelt about 1901; and Cecil Spring Rice as British ambassador, about 1913 (all Library of Congress).

A hundred and twenty-five years ago today, on 3 December 1901, Congress received the first annual message of President Theodore Roosevelt, what is now called the State of the Union.

He had been President for less than three months, since William McKinley's death in September. Following the custom of the day, the message went to Capitol Hill in writing and clerks read it aloud. It ran close to 20,000 words.

It opened with McKinley's assassination and moved through the trusts, labor, immigration, the Navy and the Philippines. Then it spent pages on trees and water.

"The forest and water problems are perhaps the most vital internal questions of the United States."

Roosevelt asked Congress to protect the forest reserves, explaining that "The fundamental idea of forestry is the perpetuation of forests by use." He argued the reserves "should be set apart forever for the use and benefit of our people as a whole and not sacrificed to the shortsighted greed of a few." And he called for the federal government to build storage and irrigation works in the arid West, where, he wrote, "it is water, not land, which measures production."

The former Dakota rancher also singled out the damage done to the reserves by overgrazing.

Congress passed the Reclamation Act the following June. Over the next seven years came a vastly expanded national forest system, the first federal bird reservations and the first national monuments, the heart of his conservation record.

On 4 December 1907, President Roosevelt ordered federal troops to Goldfield, Nevada. Within a month, his own investigators reported that the governor's call for troops wasn't justified.

Goldfield was a gold-rush boomtown, and by late 1907 it was split in two: armed union miners on one side, mine owners and their armed guards on the other. Nevada had no militia. Governor John Sparks wired Washington that the state could not keep order and asked for help.

On 4 December Roosevelt ordered Gen. Frederick Funston to take regular troops from San Francisco to Goldfield. Within days about 300 soldiers were camped in Goldfield.

Roosevelt then sent three officials he trusted to see for themselves: Lawrence Murray, Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Labor; Herbert Knox Smith, the Commissioner of Corporations; and Charles P. Neill, the Commissioner of Labor. #OTD 6 Dec 1884, in the Dakota Badlands. TR's diary, in full: "Sylvane arrived with 52 ponies, spent day breaking."

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/badlands/maltese-cross

Saturday, 6 December 1884, in the Badlands of Dakota Territory, at Roosevelt's Maltese Cross outfit. His diary entry for the day, in full:

"Sylvane arrived with 52 ponies, spent day breaking."

Sylvane Ferris, his ranch partner, had gone south to Spearfish in the Black Hills to buy horses for the outfit. He came back with fifty-two head, wild and unbroken.

It was the start of a Badlands winter. A week later the diary logged temperatures ranging from 25 above to 10 below zero. Biographer Hermann Hagedorn writes that Roosevelt worked the corral alongside his men, and on 11 December the entry reads simply: "Breaking ponies."

Not everyone was eager. The next day Roosevelt sent for Bill Sewall and Will Dow, his friends from Maine, to take ponies to the Elkhorn Ranch. In Hagedorn's account, based on Sewall's recollections, Sewall refused to try the bronco-busting: "I don't want to be pounded on the frozen ground."

Roosevelt never claimed to be a great horseman. In his Autobiography he wrote, "I never became a good roper, nor more than an average rider, according to ranch standards." When there was time, he said, he broke his own horses "gently and gradually." Fifty-two cayuses arriving in December didn't leave much time.

Shown here: Roosevelt's diary page for 6 December 1884 (Library of Congress), and the Maltese Cross cabin as it stood in his ranching days, with Sylvane Ferris in the wagon (Houghton Library, Harvard University).

#OTD 7 December 1908: Theodore Roosevelt proclaims Wheeler National Monument in Colorado's San Juan Mountains, setting aside volcanic spires "of unusual scientific interest."

No proper road was ever built to it. In 1950 Congress abolished the monument and returned it to the Forest Service. Today it's the Wheeler Geologic Area, still a hike or a rough 4x4 ride away.

On 7 December 1908, Theodore Roosevelt protected a place so hard to reach that, four decades later, Congress gave up on it.

High in the San Juan Mountains of southern Colorado, layers of volcanic ash from ancient eruptions of the La Garita caldera had worn into a maze of pale spires, pinnacles and narrow gorges. They took their name from George M. Wheeler, an Army lieutenant whose survey mapped the region in the 1870s. Under the Antiquities Act, Proclamation 831 set them aside as "of unusual scientific interest." Wheeler National Monument was Colorado's first.

There was no road to it, only trails for hikers and horses. One was proposed but never built. Visitors increasingly wanted places they could drive to; in 1943 Wheeler recorded just 43 visits.

In 1933 the monument passed to the National Park Service, which had no money to develop it. On 3 August 1950, Congress abolished it and returned the land to the Forest Service. It is one of eleven national monuments Congress has done away with.

The rocks didn't go anywhere. Today they are protected as the Wheeler Geologic Area in the Rio Grande National Forest, within the La Garita Wilderness. Getting there still takes effort: a trail of about seven miles, or a rough 14-mile four-wheel-drive road.

Shown here: the Wheeler formations (photos by John Fowler, CC BY 2.0) and President Roosevelt at his desk, 29 February 1908 (Library of Congress).

#OTD 9 Dec 1897: TR thanks C. Hart Merriam for naming the Olympic elk Cervus roosevelti after him. In 1909 he protected much of its range as Mount Olympus National Monument.

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/presidency/conservation/national-monuments

On 9 December 1897, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy wrote to thank a friend for naming an elk after him.

The friend was C. Hart Merriam, chief of the government's Biological Survey and one of the country's leading experts on mammals. The elk lived in the rain-soaked Olympic Mountains of Washington.

They looked different from the elk of the Rockies, and Roosevelt had helped spot the difference. At the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, he looked over mounted elk heads in the Oregon exhibit and told Merriam they weren't the same animal. Merriam later wrote that Roosevelt pointed out they were "black" and had "antlers with relatively straight beams."

In the summer of 1897 Merriam arranged with two trappers on the Hoh River to collect a specimen. When a big bull reached the National Museum that fall, he wrote it up as a new species and gave it a name: Cervus roosevelti. "I deem it a privilege to name this splendid animal Roosevelt's Wapiti," he wrote.

Roosevelt wrote back that he deeply appreciated the compliment, and was only sorry it would never be in his power to do anything "except to just merely appreciate it" in return.

He was wrong. On 2 March 1909, two days before he left the White House, President Roosevelt proclaimed Mount Olympus National Monument, more than 600,000 acres. The proclamation named the reason: the region had long been "the summer range and breeding grounds of the Olympic Elk (Cervus roosevelti), a species peculiar to these mountains and rapidly decreasing in numbers." In 1938 the monument became the heart of Olympic National Park, where Roosevelt elk still graze the Hoh Rain Forest.

#OTD 120 years ago, 10 Dec 1906: TR is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in ending the Russo-Japanese War, the first American to win any Nobel. He set the prize money aside for industrial peace, and later gave it to war relief.

A hundred and twenty years ago today, on 10 December 1906, Theodore Roosevelt was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. He was the first American to win a Nobel Prize of any kind.

The prize honored his role in ending the Russo-Japanese War. In August 1905 he brought the Russian and Japanese envoys together aboard the presidential yacht Mayflower at Oyster Bay, then kept the talks from collapsing until the two sides signed the Treaty of Portsmouth that September.

Roosevelt didn't go to the ceremony in Christiania, now Oslo. The American minister to Norway, Herbert H. D. Peirce, accepted for him and read a telegram from the President:

"I am profoundly moved and touched by the signal honor shown me through your body in conferring upon me the Nobel Peace Prize."

He gave the credit away: "for what I did, I was able to accomplish only as the representative of the nation of which, for the time being, I am president."

Then he gave the money away, too. The prize came to about $37,000, and he set it aside to found "a permanent industrial peace committee" in Washington, to work for better relations between employers and wage workers. A foundation was set up, but its trustees never put the money to work. With the fund still unspent, Roosevelt asked Congress to return it, and in August 1918 he gave it to war relief, including the American Red Cross, the YMCA, the Knights of Columbus, the Jewish Welfare Board and the Salvation Army.

He did make it to Norway eventually. On 5 May 1910, on his way home from Africa, he delivered his Nobel address in Christiania.

#OTD 12 Dec 1884: In bitter Badlands cold, TR sets out after bighorn sheep. On the third day, after a tramp through "the roughest kind of ground," he got his ram and galloped home in a blizzard.

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/badlands/maltese-cross

On 12 December 1884, in a cold snap that had frozen the Little Missouri solid, Theodore Roosevelt set out from his Maltese Cross ranch after bighorn sheep.

Winter had come hard to the Badlands. The river, he wrote later, "lay fixed like a huge bent bar of blue steel." The men were working a bunch of half-broken ponies, and one of the cowboys made what Roosevelt called "a funny mistake": he spotted two dark ponies and "had mistaken them for bears."

His diary for the 12th is brisk: "George in buckboard, Merrifield and I on horseback started on sheep hunt." George Myers drove the buckboard with the camp gear. Bill Merrifield, Roosevelt's ranch partner, rode alongside. They rode and walked all day over ice-glazed buttes, saw nothing and slept in a deserted hunter's shack on a bend of the river.

The next day was no better. "Tramped all over Bullion's Butte; saw nothing," he wrote. The thermometer swung from 25 above zero to 10 below.

On the third day, 14 December, they rode three miles and then went on foot through "the roughest kind of ground." He "came on a Bighorn ram and shot him at about 90 yards." They galloped the last mile with a blizzard in their faces.

He wrote to his sister Anna that he had tramped "over the most awful country that can be imagined" and added: "I have now killed every kind of plains game." The next year he told the whole story in Hunting Trips of a Ranchman, in a chapter called "A Trip After Mountain Sheep."

Shown here: the butte across the Little Missouri from the Elkhorn ranch house, about 1886, probably photographed by or for Roosevelt (Houghton Library, Harvard University); the opening page of "A Trip After Mountain Sheep," from Hunting Trips of a Ranchman, 1885 (Biodiversity Heritage Library); and Roosevelt with his old Badlands companions Bill Merrifield, Sylvane and Joe Ferris, and George Myers, Chicago, August 1912 (Houghton Library, Harvard University).

On 13 December 1904, President Theodore Roosevelt wrote to his old boxing teacher, Mike Donovan, with a report on his afternoon.

He had been sparring and fencing with singlesticks, he wrote, with his son Ted, Ted's football friend and a couple of young army officers. Then came the bad news: "I am sorry to say I have wrenched my thigh again and succeeded in breaking a blood vessel in one eye."

The note made it sound minor. It was not.

Years later, in his Autobiography (1913), he described boxing with some of his aides while President: "in one bout a young captain of artillery cross-countered me on the eye, and the blow smashed the little blood-vessels. Fortunately it was my left eye, but the sight has been dim ever since, and if it had been the right eye I should have been entirely unable to shoot."

He never named the young officer in print. Biographers have identified him as Dan T. Moore, a White House military aide and a cousin of Edith Roosevelt. When the news spread in 1917, Moore told a Washington newspaper he had never known.

The sight in that eye faded over the years; by the end of his life he could see little more than light with it. He went on riding, hiking, hunting and exploring anyway.

#OTD 14 Dec 1905: Front pages announce Alice Roosevelt's engagement to Rep. Nicholas Longworth. She said they announced it because "the papers were daily doing it for us." They wed at the White House in Feb. 1906.

On 14 December 1905, front pages across the country carried the news: Alice Roosevelt was engaged.

The President and Mrs. Roosevelt had made the formal announcement late the afternoon before. Alice, 21, would marry Nicholas Longworth, 36, a congressman from Cincinnati. New Haven's Daily Morning Journal and Courier ran it on the front page and predicted the wedding would take place "about the middle of next February" and that it was expected to "occur at the White House."

They had grown close that summer on a long official trip to Asia led by Secretary of War William Howard Taft. By the time the couple made it official, the press was already ahead of them.

Alice told it this way in her memoir, Crowded Hours (1933): "Nick and I decided that we were engaged and that we might as well announce our engagement, as the papers were daily doing it for us."

She broke the news to her stepmother, Edith, in the bathroom. "Nick, meanwhile, with great formality was announcing it to Father in the study."

The paper got the wedding right. Alice Roosevelt and Nicholas Longworth were married in the East Room of the White House on 17 February 1906.

#OTD 120 years ago today, 15 December 1906: President Roosevelt presents Commander Robert E. Peary the National Geographic Society's first Hubbard Medal, for his record claim of "Farthest north, 87° 6'."

Peary's ship was named the Roosevelt. Matthew Henson and Inuit hunters from Greenland were essential to the expedition. Peary's later claim to the North Pole is still debated.

A hundred and twenty years ago today, on 15 December 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt handed Commander Robert E. Peary the first Hubbard Medal ever awarded by the National Geographic Society.

About 400 members and guests filled the New Willard Hotel in Washington for the Society's annual banquet. Tiffany & Co. had struck the medal for the occasion. Its inscription read "Farthest north, 87° 6'" for the record Peary claimed that April, and a blue sapphire star from Montana marked the spot.

Roosevelt arrived after dinner had been served, in the middle of a speech by the explorer Frederick A. Cook. When his turn came, he singled out "the work of the explorer, who faces and overcomes perils and hardships which the average soldier never in his life knows."

Peary's ship carried the President's name: the Roosevelt. In his reply, Peary, speaking for the Peary Arctic Club, thanked the President for his "permission to name the club's ship after you."

Peary was not alone in the Arctic. Matthew Henson, the African American explorer who went north with him on expedition after expedition, sailed on the Roosevelt in 1905 and 1906, and Inuit families from northwest Greenland did much of the hunting and sledging that made the push north possible.

Three years later, Peary and Cook both claimed to have reached the North Pole. Cook's claim was widely rejected. Peary's has been argued over ever since.

#OTD 16 December 1907: From the presidential yacht Mayflower, Theodore Roosevelt watches sixteen white-hulled battleships steam out of Hampton Roads, Virginia, bound around the world.

The Great White Fleet covered about 43,000 miles in 14 months. Roosevelt called it "the most important service that I rendered to peace."

On 16 December 1907, sixteen American battleships, their hulls painted white, steamed out of Hampton Roads, Virginia. President Theodore Roosevelt watched them go from the presidential yacht Mayflower.

They were headed around the world. Under Rear Admiral Robley D. Evans (Rear Admiral Charles S. Sperry took command at San Francisco), some 14,000 sailors set out on a voyage of about 43,000 miles, with 20 port calls on six continents.

Roosevelt later wrote that he made the decision without consulting his Cabinet. He wanted the world to see that the Navy could shift its battleships from the Atlantic to the Pacific whenever it chose. He also claimed that neither the British nor the German naval authorities believed an American battleship fleet could make the trip.

Relations with Japan were strained at the time, and critics warned that Japan would see the cruise as a threat. Roosevelt said privately he did not believe it would. When the fleet reached Japan in October 1908, it was welcomed with celebrations.

He was clear about his main audience. In his Autobiography he wrote: "My prime purpose was to impress the American people; and this purpose was fully achieved." He believed nothing had done more to build public interest in the Navy.

The fleet came home to Hampton Roads on 22 February 1909, Washington's Birthday, and Roosevelt was there to greet it. He left office ten days later. Looking back, he wrote: "In my own judgment the most important service that I rendered to peace was the voyage of the battle fleet round the world."

On 17 December 1904, a snowy Saturday in Washington, President Theodore Roosevelt wrote to his son Kermit, 15 and away at Groton School in Massachusetts.

For a week, he reported, it had been "down to zero at night." He had been too busy to ride until after dark, so he rode by moonlight: "the moonlight on the glittering snow made the rides lovelier than they would have been in the daytime."

There was news from home. "The new black 'Jack' dog is becoming very much at home and very fond of the family." Ted, 17, was going out "very swell in his first tail coat."

And there was this, from a President who had just won a full term of his own: "With Archie and Quentin I have finished 'The Last of the Mohicans,' and have now begun 'The Deerslayer.'" Archie was 10. Quentin was 7.

Reading to them in the evening, he wrote, "gives me a chance to see them that I would not otherwise have, although sometimes it is rather hard to get time."

He signed off with news Kermit was surely waiting for: "In a very few days now we shall see you again."

The letter appears in Theodore Roosevelt's Letters to His Children, published in 1919.

#OTD 18 Dec 1908: TR asks that the lions' heads on the White House State Dining Room mantel be swapped for bison, "a much more characteristic and American decoration." A replica went back in 1962.

On 18 December 1908, with less than three months left in his presidency, Theodore Roosevelt wrote to the architects who had remodeled the White House. He had a request about the fireplace in the State Dining Room.

When McKim, Mead & White enlarged the room in 1902, its big stone mantel was carved with lions' heads. Roosevelt wanted them replaced. In his letter to William M. Kendall of the firm, he asked for stone bison heads instead, calling them "a much more characteristic and American decoration." He wanted the work done quickly.

The lions came off. American bison went on.

The timing was apt. By then the bison had already been hunted nearly to extinction. In the fall of 1907, fifteen bison from the New York Zoological Park had been shipped west to restock the Wichita National Forest and Game Preserve in Oklahoma Territory.

The bison mantel outlasted Roosevelt's White House. It was removed during the Truman reconstruction of 1949 to 1952, and the original went to the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri. In 1962, the Kennedys installed a replica in the State Dining Room, bison heads and all.

Shown here: the State Dining Room mantel in March 1903, from a stereograph; the State Dining Room about 1904 (both Library of Congress); and the mantel about 1948, shortly before it was removed (Harry S. Truman Library).

#OTD 19 Dec 1884: Little Missouri cattlemen meet in Medora and elect TR, 26, chairman of their new stockmen's association. Later tales made it an armed showdown. Hagedorn called it "no more exciting than a sewing-circle."

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/badlands/frontier-life

On 19 December 1884, cattlemen from up and down the Little Missouri gathered in Medora, Dakota Territory, with Theodore Roosevelt, 26, presiding.

Later storytellers turned that day into a showdown: armed men bursting in, a crooked deputy marshal, Roosevelt staring them all down. Hermann Hagedorn, who interviewed Roosevelt's Badlands neighbors for his 1921 history, Roosevelt in the Bad Lands, called the story's authenticity dubious. The meeting, he concluded, was "dramatic only in its implications and no more exciting than a sewing-circle."

What happened is in the minutes of the meeting, now at Harvard's Houghton Library.

The stockmen resolved to form an association of "the Stockmen along the Little Missouri and its tributaries" and elected Roosevelt chairman. They adopted bylaws. They named the Marquis de Morès, Medora's founder, a "Committee of One" to work with the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association for laws from the territorial legislature that would favor cattlemen. Gregor Lang, one of the Marquis's sharpest critics, sat in the same room.

Billings County existed on paper but was not yet organized. The new association bound its members to mutual protection "against frauds and swindlers" and stock thieves, with a young New Yorker in the chair.

Roosevelt planned to start for home the next day, and he reached New York a day or two before Christmas.

Shown here: Medora in 1883, with the office and company store of the Marquis de Morès, and the Little Missouri, about 1886, photographed by Roosevelt (both Houghton Library, Harvard University).

#OTD 20 Dec 1906: As the Colorado River floods the Salton Sink, TR wires E. H. Harriman: "It is incumbent upon you to close break again." Harriman's railroad crews closed it in Feb. 1907.

On 20 December 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt sent a blunt telegram to the railroad magnate E. H. Harriman about a river that had run away.

In 1904, a private irrigation company cut a canal intake through the bank of the Colorado River, on the Mexican side of the border, to water farms in California's Imperial Valley. In 1905 the floods tore the cut wide open. Nearly the whole river swung west and poured downhill into the Salton Sink, a desert basin far below sea level, and a lake began to spread across it. Farms, towns and the Southern Pacific's tracks were in the way.

Harriman's Southern Pacific, which had lent the company money, closed the break on 4 November 1906. A month later, high water broke through again.

Harriman wanted the government to take over. Roosevelt answered that the Reclamation Service could not start work "without authority of Congress and suitable convention with Mexico," and Congress was adjourning that very day for the holidays. "It is incumbent upon you to close break again," he wired.

Harriman replied the same day. The irrigation company was not a Southern Pacific enterprise, he pointed out, but he ordered his men to start at once and trusted the government to help with the cost later.

Crews drove trestles across the gap, and trains dumped rock into the current faster than it could wash away. On 10 February 1907, the Colorado went back into its old channel.

Roosevelt later urged Congress to repay the railroad, and so did President Taft. Congress let the bill die. Not until 1929 did the railroad win about $1 million, through the Court of Claims.

The lake the flood left behind is still there, fed today mostly by farm runoff: the Salton Sea.

On 21 December 1901, the War Department made public a reprimand of the highest-ranking officer in the United States Army.

Lieutenant General Nelson A. Miles had commanded the Army since 1895. He was a Civil War hero and Medal of Honor recipient. He and the new President, in office a little over three months, had little use for each other.

That December, the Navy was caught up in a bitter quarrel over Rear Admiral Winfield Scott Schley's conduct in the 1898 Santiago campaign, and over whether he or Rear Admiral William T. Sampson deserved credit for the victory. A naval court of inquiry had just issued its findings, with Admiral George Dewey dissenting on some points. Miles told a newspaper interviewer in Cincinnati that he was willing to take Dewey's judgment.

Secretary of War Elihu Root, writing "by direction of the President," called Miles's explanation "not satisfactory." "It is of no consequence on whose side your opinion was or what it was," Root wrote. "You had no business in the controversy and no right, holding the office which you did, to express any opinion."

In other words, the Army's commander had no business taking sides in public on a Navy dispute.

Miles also called at the White House, where, according to some reports, Roosevelt rebuked him sharply in front of other callers. One witness, the journalist Henry V. Boynton, insisted the President had not been rude. Some newspapers thought the President had been too hard on an old soldier.

Miles retired in 1903, the last officer to hold the title Commanding General of the Army. Congress replaced the post with a Chief of Staff.

On 23 December 1911, Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter that historians still quote when they explain the most dramatic political year of his life.

He had been out of the White House for almost three years. His friendship with his successor, William Howard Taft, had come apart, and progressive Republicans were urging him to run again in 1912. To William B. Howland, an officer of The Outlook, the magazine where Roosevelt was a contributing editor, he wrote in a private letter:

"I am not a candidate, I will never be a candidate; but I have to tell the La Follette men and the Taft men that while I am absolutely sincere in saying that I am not a candidate and do not wish the nomination, yet that I do not feel it would be right or proper for me to say that under no circumstances would I accept it if it came..."

Not a candidate, then. But not a closed door, either.

In late February 1912, he announced that he would accept the Republican nomination if it were offered. The contest that followed split the party and gave rise to the Progressive, or Bull Moose, Party.

The same day he wrote to Howland, Roosevelt sent his son Archie, away at school in Arizona, the family news: "Quentin turned up last night. He is half an inch taller than I am, and is in great shape."

#OTD 125 years ago, 24 Dec 1901: First White House Christmas Eve for the Roosevelts. No tree, but Thomas Nast drew Santa at the mantel beside six stockings. And there's no evidence TR "banned" trees.

A hundred and twenty-five years ago today, on 24 December 1901, the Roosevelts spent their first Christmas Eve in the White House. Theodore Roosevelt had been President for just over three months, and six children, ages 4 to 17, had moved in with him and Edith.

There was no Christmas tree. Newspapers reported that a tree had never been part of the family's Christmas, and that Mrs. Roosevelt could not spare a single room for one anyway. The children had their tree at the home of an aunt and uncle instead.

What the White House did have was stockings. In 1901, the cartoonist Thomas Nast, who did as much as anyone to shape America's picture of Santa Claus, drew him beside a White House mantel hung with six stockings, each labeled with a Roosevelt child's name. Nast called it "New Life in the Old House." Santa says, "I dont know when I've felt so at home here!"

In later White House years, Roosevelt described the family routine in his letters: stockings opened on their parents' bed early on Christmas morning, then bigger presents in the library after breakfast.

You may have heard that Roosevelt banned Christmas trees to save the forests. The White House Historical Association and the Forest History Society call the ban a myth. The family simply didn't have the habit. (A year later, Archie set up a little tree of his own in a closet as a surprise.)

On Christmas morning 1918, Theodore Roosevelt went home.

He had spent most of November and December in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid low by inflammatory rheumatism. An inflamed inner ear left him dizzy, and doctors warned he might spend much of the rest of his life in a wheelchair. Five months earlier, his youngest son, Quentin, had been shot down and killed over France.

Still, he was well enough to go home for Christmas. He was dizzy as he stepped out of the hospital elevator, and his physician, Dr. John H. Richards, took his arm. Roosevelt stopped him. "Don't do that," he said, as the doctor later recalled. He was not sick, he insisted, and help would "give the wrong impression." He walked out to the waiting car on his own, Edith at his side.

At Sagamore Hill, Alice, Ethel, Archie and Archie's wife, Grace, were waiting, along with his grandchildren. He watched his little granddaughter Edie Derby run around the drawing room, but by afternoon he was worn out.

Twelve days later, on 6 January 1919, he died in his sleep at Sagamore Hill. It was his last Christmas.

On 26 December 1908, with ten weeks left in the White House, Theodore Roosevelt got the best news of his holiday season.

He was planning a year-long expedition to East Africa to collect specimens for the Smithsonian Institution, and for months he had been trading letters with Frederick Courteney Selous, the English hunter and naturalist whose books on African wildlife he had read for years. Now Selous wrote that he would be making his own trip to British East Africa that spring, on the same steamer.

Roosevelt fired back: "Three cheers! I am simply overjoyed that you are going out. It is just the last touch to make everything perfect. But you must leave me one lion somewhere!"

He added that he did not really expect to get one anyhow.

He did. They met at Naples in April 1909, sailed together aboard the Admiral to Mombasa, and rode the train inland side by side on a seat across the locomotive's cowcatcher. Weeks later, Roosevelt was able to show Selous his first lions. Over the next year the Smithsonian-Roosevelt African Expedition sent thousands of specimens home to Washington, many of them still in the National Museum of Natural History's collections.

On 27 December 1904, Theodore Roosevelt sent his secretary of the Treasury a short, blunt note about the money in America's pockets.

"I think our coinage is artistically of atrocious hideousness," he wrote to Leslie M. Shaw. "Would it be possible, without asking permission of Congress, to employ a man like Saint-Gaudens to give us a coinage that would have some beauty?"

Augustus Saint-Gaudens was one of the country's most celebrated sculptors. It was possible, and the Treasury hired him. Saint-Gaudens took on the $10 and $20 gold coins, and Roosevelt backed his designs over the objections of the Mint's chief engraver, Charles Barber.

The $20 double eagle came out in 1907: Liberty striding forward with a torch and an olive branch, and on the back an eagle in flight above a rising sun. The first version, in very high relief with the date in Roman numerals, was so deep it was hard to strike and was soon flattened for regular production. Saint-Gaudens, ill with cancer, died in August 1907, before the coins went into circulation.

The design also left off "In God We Trust." Congress ordered the motto put back in 1908.

That one note set off a redesign that, by 1921, had changed every U.S. coin. Collectors still call the Saint-Gaudens double eagle one of the most beautiful American coins ever made.

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/presidency/executive-power

On 27 December 1904, Theodore Roosevelt sent his secretary of the Treasury a short, blunt note about the money in America's pockets.

"I think our coinage is artistically of atrocious hideousness," he wrote to Leslie M. Shaw. "Would it be possible, without asking permission of Congress, to employ a man like Saint-Gaudens to give us a coinage that would have some beauty?"

Augustus Saint-Gaudens was one of the country's most celebrated sculptors. It was possible, and the Treasury hired him. Saint-Gaudens took on the $10 and $20 gold coins, and Roosevelt backed his designs over the objections of the Mint's chief engraver, Charles Barber.

The $20 double eagle came out in 1907: Liberty striding forward with a torch and an olive branch, and on the back an eagle in flight above a rising sun. The first version, in very high relief with the date in Roman numerals, was so deep it was hard to strike and was soon flattened for regular production. Saint-Gaudens, ill with cancer, died in August 1907, before the coins went into circulation.

The design also left off "In God We Trust." Congress ordered the motto put back in 1908.

That one note set off a redesign that, by 1921, had changed every U.S. coin. Collectors still call the Saint-Gaudens double eagle one of the most beautiful American coins ever made.

Shown here: a 1907 high-relief double eagle (National Numismatic Collection, Smithsonian, photographed by Jaclyn Nash); and Secretary Shaw at his desk, 1905 (G. G. Bain, Library of Congress).

On 28 December 1904, the White House offered to host a wedding.

The bride was Eleanor Roosevelt, 20, daughter of the President's late brother, Elliott. Her mother had died when she was 8, and her father less than two years later. Earlier that month her engagement had been announced to a distant cousin, a 22-year-old Columbia law student named Franklin Delano Roosevelt.

Edith Roosevelt wrote to Eleanor offering to send out the invitations and hold the ceremony at the White House, doing for her just what they would do for their own daughter Alice. The President, she explained, felt that on that day he would stand in her father's place.

Eleanor said no, thank you. She wanted something smaller.

She and Franklin married on 17 March 1905, St. Patrick's Day, in two adjoining family houses on East 76th Street in New York. The President, in town for the St. Patrick's Day parade, gave the bride away.

Twenty-eight years later, Eleanor moved into the White House after all, as First Lady.

Shown here: Eleanor Roosevelt in her wedding dress, 1905 (Pach Brothers, National Archives); and Edith Roosevelt, February 1905 (Library of Congress).

On 29 December 1913, deep in Brazil's Mato Grosso, Theodore Roosevelt's diary for the day recorded: "Killed peccary with spear."

He was 55, a year past losing the 1912 election, and already on the expedition that would take him down the uncharted River of Doubt. He had arrived at the São João ranch the day before and was hunting the marshes with his son Kermit and their Brazilian hosts.

That morning the dogs bayed two peccaries, small, pig-like animals of the Brazilian marshes and forests, in a hollow log. The two broke out the far end and vanished into the tangle. Twenty minutes later the pack had the boar cornered in a half-hollow stump, the dogs crowded so close around its head that a rifle shot was out of the question. So Roosevelt borrowed a spear from his host's son and killed the boar by hand.

In Through the Brazilian Wilderness he called the animal "a valiant and truculent little beast," one that would take a teacup-sized bite out of a man or a dog if it got the chance.

An hour or two later the dogs struck the fresh trail of two jaguars, and a sudden downpour washed it out. Two months after that, the expedition started down the River of Doubt, the hardest journey of his life.

Shown here: Roosevelt and Col. Cândido Rondon (right) with a jaguar skin, Brazil, 1913; and Roosevelt seated in a boat during the expedition (both photographed by Kermit Roosevelt; Library of Congress).

#OTD 30 December 1910: Theodore Roosevelt answers Senator Robert La Follette's invitation to put his name on the new National Progressive Republican League. He hesitates and asks to talk it over in person. The League launches without him, and a little over a year later the two men are rivals for the Republican nomination.

In a letter the Library of Congress dates to 30 December 1910, Theodore Roosevelt answered Senator Robert M. La Follette of Wisconsin, and held back.

La Follette and Senator Jonathan Bourne of Oregon were about to launch the National Progressive Republican League. Its program aimed to hand voters more direct power: popular election of U.S. senators, direct primaries, and the initiative, referendum and recall. They wanted the former president's name on the call.

Roosevelt wrote that he was hesitant to sign it, and asked to talk the matter over in person.

In the end he stayed out. La Follette wrote that he regretted Roosevelt's decision, and on 21 January 1911 the League was organized in Washington without him. Days later Roosevelt explained that he was sympathetic to much of the program but did not want a prominent part in any political movement; as a former president, he said, he was trying to take part in politics as a private citizen. He offered instead to endorse the League in The Outlook, the magazine where he was a contributing editor.

A little over a year later the two men were rivals. In February 1912, speaking to the Ohio constitutional convention in Columbus, Roosevelt came out for the initiative and the referendum and for the recall of certain court decisions, and within days he was a candidate for the Republican nomination himself.

Shown here: Senator Robert M. La Follette, 1911; and Roosevelt speaking at Missouri Valley, Iowa, 21 August 1910 (both Library of Congress).

#OTD 31 December 1883: Theodore Roosevelt, 25, goes into the Republican caucus in Albany expecting to be chosen Speaker of the New York Assembly. Pledged votes slip away to Titus Sheard and he loses. He moves to make Sheard's nomination unanimous, and later writes that the defeat "materially strengthened my position."

On 31 December 1883, Theodore Roosevelt, 25, went into the Republican caucus in Albany expecting to be chosen Speaker of the New York State Assembly. He came out beaten.

Republicans had just won control of the Assembly, so the caucus pick would become Speaker the next day. Roosevelt had spent weeks lining up votes. By late afternoon a rival had dropped out, and he looked to have enough.

Then, in the hours before the evening caucus, the party organization went to work. Bosses from both Republican factions, President Arthur's Stalwarts and Senator Warner Miller's Half-Breeds, combined behind Titus Sheard, a former Assemblyman from Herkimer County. Pledged votes slipped away to Sheard, the New York City members among them, and Roosevelt lost on the first ballot.

He moved to make Sheard's nomination unanimous.

"I was much chagrined for the moment," he later wrote in his Autobiography. Looking back, he decided the loss had helped: "My defeat in the end materially strengthened my position, and enabled me to accomplish far more than I could have accomplished as Speaker."

Sheard gave him the chairmanship of the Cities Committee, and he spent the session on reform bills for New York City. Six weeks later, on 14 February 1884, his mother and his wife Alice died in the same house, hours apart.

Shown here: Roosevelt as a New York Assemblyman, early 1880s (Houghton Library, Harvard University); and the Assembly Chamber of the New York State Capitol, Albany, date unknown (Library of Congress).

#OTD 1 January 1907, 120 years ago today: Theodore Roosevelt opens the White House to anyone willing to wait in line and shakes hands for hours. Guinness World Records lists 8,513, a record for a head of state, though newspapers at the time counted anywhere from about 5,000 to nearly 10,000. Happy New Year!

A hundred and twenty years ago today, on 1 January 1907, the White House opened its doors, and Theodore Roosevelt shook hands with everyone willing to wait in line.

The New Year's Day reception was open to the public. Diplomats, officials and military officers came through first; then the gates opened to everyone else. Roosevelt stood in the Blue Room and greeted callers one after another for hours.

How many hands did he shake? Guinness World Records lists 8,513, the most handshakes by a head of state. The papers at the time could not agree: one Washington count gave about 5,000 callers, the Associated Press about 8,500, and another paper nearly 10,000. Whatever the number, he did it in a single day.

The open-house tradition lasted another quarter century. Herbert Hoover cancelled the reception in 1933, and no president has revived it.

Happy New Year from the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library.

Shown here: Admiral George Dewey and Navy officers in line for Roosevelt's New Year's reception, 1902 (Underwood & Underwood stereograph); and the White House Blue Room, where Roosevelt received his callers, about 1902 (B. M. Clinedinst) (both Library of Congress).
